common_name: Choppee Okra (South Carolina Lowcountry Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is reliably warm; Choppee is a South Carolina Lowcountry heirloom named for the community along the Black River, prized for its early, heavy-yielding, nearly spineless pods.

directions: Direct sow seed an inch deep after the soil has warmed, spacing plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Choppee is an heirloom okra passed down among South Carolina Lowcountry gardening families near the Choppee community in Georgetown County, valued for producing tender, nearly spineless, slightly ridged green pods with a reddish tinge at the base earlier in the season than many other Southern heirlooms. The plants are productive and well adapted to the humid, hot conditions of the coastal Southeast, and pods should be picked at 3-5 inches for the best table quality. Like most heirloom okras it is open-pollinated and easily saved from year to year, helping preserve a piece of Lowcountry foodways history.
sources: Slow Food USA Ark of Taste

common_name: Eagle Pass Okra (South Texas Heirloom Okra)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed thoroughly; Eagle Pass is a Texas borderland heirloom valued for exceptional heat and drought tolerance, well suited to South Texas and other hot, dry summer gardens.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep once soil is thoroughly warm, since this variety germinates poorly in cool soil; space plants 12-18 inches apart in full sun. Eagle Pass is a Texas heirloom okra originating from the border region around Eagle Pass, Texas, selected over generations for tolerance of extreme heat and limited water, making it a strong performer in South Texas and other arid warm-climate gardens where many other okra varieties struggle. Plants grow tall and produce ribbed green pods that should be harvested young, at around 3-4 inches, for best tenderness. It remains a favorite among regional seed savers for its resilience and reliable yields under harsh summer conditions.

common_name: Chicago Pickling Cucumber (1888 Heirloom Pickling Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; Chicago Pickling is a productive 19th-century heirloom bred specifically for commercial and home pickle production, still favored for its high yields of blocky, uniform fruit.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in hills or rows after the soil has warmed, and provide a trellis or ample vine room. Chicago Pickling dates to the late 1880s and was long a mainstay of Midwestern commercial pickle production, producing an abundant crop of medium-green, black-spined fruit that holds its blocky shape well through brining and fermentation. Pick fruit small, at around 2-4 inches, for classic dill and bread-and-butter pickles, and harvest frequently to keep the vigorous vines setting new fruit. Because it is open-pollinated, gardeners can save seed season to season, continuing a variety with over a century of documented use in American home and commercial pickling.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Wisconsin SMR 58 was bred at the University of Wisconsin for scab and mosaic resistance and remains a widely grown standard open-pollinated pickling cucumber.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep after the soil has warmed, in fertile, well-drained soil with room for vines to spread or climb a trellis. Wisconsin SMR 58, standing for Smooth or Spot Mosaic Resistant, descends from a University of Wisconsin breeding program that improved disease resistance in the older Wisconsin SMR line, becoming a standard pickling cucumber for home gardeners and small-scale growers because of its reliable yields, disease tolerance, and dependable performance across varied soils. Fruit is straight, blocky, and medium green with light spines, best picked young at 2-4 inches for pickles or left a bit larger for fresh slicing. Because it remains true from seed, it can be maintained by home seed savers who isolate it from other cucumber varieties.

common_name: Little Leaf Cucumber (H-19, Beetle-Resistant Pickling Cucumber)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil is warm; this Cornell-bred pickling cucumber has unusually small leaves that reduce cucumber beetle damage and improve airflow, making it a favorite for organic growers.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants to allow good air circulation. Little Leaf, formally H-19, was developed by Cornell University plant breeders specifically for its diminutive foliage, a trait that exposes fewer leaf surfaces to cucumber beetles and their associated bacterial wilt while still allowing plenty of sunlight to reach developing fruit and improving disease airflow around the vines. It is gynoecious, so interplanting with a small percentage of a standard pollenizer variety, or relying on nearby bees for cross-pollination from other varieties, improves fruit set. Fruits are small, blocky, and dark green, ideal for classic dill pickles, and should be harvested every one to two days at 2-4 inches for best quality.
sources: Cornell University College of Agriculture and Life Sciences

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm soil; Parisian Pickling is a classic French cornichon-type cucumber grown for tiny, crisp fruit harvested daily at just an inch or two for traditional French pickles.

directions: Direct sow an inch deep after last frost in warm, fertile soil, and provide a low trellis or ample ground space for the compact vines. Parisian Pickling is a traditional French cornichon cucumber grown for centuries around Paris and other French market gardens, producing an abundance of small, bumpy, dark green fruit that must be picked daily, often at under two inches long, to catch them at the ideal size for classic French cornichon pickles served alongside pâté and charcuterie. The vines are prolific once picking begins in earnest, since frequent harvest of the smallest fruit encourages continuous new fruit set through the season. Flavor is crisp and mild even at the smallest sizes, distinguishing true cornichon types from cucumbers merely picked young.
